title: Security review: Usage Insights exports (audit logs + RBAC) - Redwood Inference x Meridian Capital Markets
summary: Meridian Capital Markets requested a focused security/compliance review on the new in-console Usage Insights export feature (CSV/JSON). Customer questions centered on: what audit events are emitted for export creation/download, required audit fields for evidence, RBAC/tenant isolation boundaries (org/project/env/region), data residency and retention for exported artifacts, and whether exports can be disabled or constrained. Redwood explained export flow (job creation -> async generation -> time-limited download), audit log event coverage (create/download/failure), and that all insights/export APIs enforce org/project scoping. Follow-ups include sharing the audit event field list and confirming retention/region behavior for export objects for their regulated environment.
topics: Audit logging for export actions; RBAC boundaries for usage insights; compliance evidence (SOC 2, access logs); export retention + download link expiry; data residency; least-privilege roles; console vs API access; rate limits and size limits for exports; invoice reconciliation expectations.
questions: Do you log both export job creation and file download? What fields are in the audit log (filters/time range/project)? Can a project admin export cross-project data? Where is the exported file stored and for how long? Can we restrict exports entirely? Are exports included in SOC 2 evidence and can we retrieve audit logs via API?
next_steps: Redwood to send Meridian the Usage Insights export audit event schema + example entries (create/download) for their evidence checklist.
Meridian to confirm their required retention for audit logs and whether they need export artifact retention > 7 days (Redwood recommendation is short-lived artifacts).
Redwood to confirm data residency behavior for export artifacts in Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private and share a one-paragraph statement suitable for GRC.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up with Platform Eng to review RBAC roles/permissions mapping and whether a custom role is needed.
action_items: Owner: Kevin Osei — Provide sample audit log events for usage report export (job_created, download_started/completed, job_failed) with field definitions by 2026-02-13.
Owner: Marcus Lin — Confirm export artifact retention + link TTL defaults and whether they are configurable per org by 2026-02-14.
Owner: Naomi Feldman — Send SOC 2 coverage statement and point to audit log retrieval options (console + API) by 2026-02-13.
Owner: Logan Wright — Clarify RBAC enforcement points in insights APIs (org/project/env/region) and any known edge cases by 2026-02-14.
Owner: Priya Desai — Share Meridian’s internal control requirements for “data export” category (who can export / approvals) by 2026-02-17.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Security review: Usage Insights exports (audit logs + RBAC) - Redwood Inference x Meridian Capital Markets
Date: 2026-02-11
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 52 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Naomi Feldman, Marcus Lin, Kevin Osei, Logan Wright
Meridian Capital Markets: Priya Desai, Jonah Kim, Ethan Morales, Sara Nguyen

---

[00:00] Naomi Feldman: Cool. I think we’re all here. Hi everyone, I’m Naomi, I cover security product reviews on Redwood’s side. We brought Marcus from security engineering, Kevin who worked on audit logging for exports, and Logan from telemetry/analytics.

[00:12] Priya Desai: Hi. Thanks Naomi. I’m Priya, security engineering. Jonah is on GRC. Ethan is platform, and Sara is fin ops. This is mainly about the exports in that new usage insights thing.

[00:25] Naomi Feldman: Yep. The cost drivers by route and model, and the ability to export CSV or JSON from the console.

[00:33] Jonah Kim: Right. We saw in the deck it said “audited exports” and “RBAC”. We need specifics for our control evidence.

[00:44] Naomi Feldman: Totally. Maybe to frame it: are you looking at Hosted API, or Dedicated, or Private deployment?

[00:51] Ethan Morales: Likely Dedicated in a single region first, but we’re evaluating VPC later. But exports and logging should be consistent.

[01:03] Marcus Lin: Got it.

[01:05] Sara Nguyen: For me it’s like, we want to pull weekly cost by route to reconcile internally. But security wants to be sure we can track who exported what.

[01:18] Naomi Feldman: Makes sense. Let’s do audit logs first. Kevin, do you want to summarize what we emit?

[01:27] Kevin Osei: Yeah. So exports are modeled as an “export job” that you create in the console or via API. That action generates an audit log event, and then when you download the resulting file, that generates another audit log event.

[01:44] Jonah Kim: Is it just one event or two? Like “created” vs “downloaded”.

[01:48] Kevin Osei: Two, at least. The baseline is: export_job_created and export_download_initiated, and we also track export_job_failed if generation fails. Depending on the client we sometimes see “download completed” too, but the guaranteed one is the initiation.

[02:08] Priya Desai: What fields are in those events? We need actor identity, IP address, and the data scope.

[02:17] Kevin Osei: Actor identity: the Redwood user ID and the email, and if it’s via API token then the token identity maps back to a service account. We also capture org ID, project ID, and the filters used—time window, route filter, model filter, environment, region, deployment mode.

[02:37] Logan Wright: And importantly the export job ID, so you can correlate creation to the generated artifact and download.

[02:44] Priya Desai: Do you log “what rows” got exported? Like number of routes, models?

[02:49] Kevin Osei: We log a summary: requested time range and aggregation level, and the “row count” once it completes. The actual contents aren’t duplicated into the audit event.

[03:01] Jonah Kim: Okay, but we need enough evidence to show “a user exported cost data for project X for last 30 days” kind of thing.

[03:10] Naomi Feldman: That’s basically what the event is designed to provide: who, when, project/org, and the exact filters/time range.

[03:19] Ethan Morales: Does it include the route names? That might be sensitive for us.

[03:24] Kevin Osei: We do not log a full list of route values in the audit event. We log the filter expression. If you exported “all routes” it says that. If you filtered to a single route, it might store that route string; we can confirm the exact behavior because there are some normalization rules.

[03:43] Marcus Lin: And to be clear, route strings should be normalized anyway—like avoid user IDs in route. That’s more of a telemetry cardinality guideline, but it also helps with sensitive leakage.

[03:55] Priya Desai: That’s actually one of our questions. Route names can include customer identifiers if engineers are sloppy.

[04:03] Logan Wright: Yeah. We have guardrails. There’s length limits and allowed character sets, and we recommend templated names like “/v1/chat/completions” not “/user/12345/chat”.

[04:15] Priya Desai: Okay. RBAC. Can a project admin export data across projects?

[04:22] Marcus Lin: No. The insights APIs and the export job creation endpoint are scoped to org and project. The server checks your membership and role for that project.

[04:33] Jonah Kim: What about like environments? Prod vs staging.

[04:36] Marcus Lin: Environments are dimensions inside a project. You can filter by environment, but the permission boundary is still the project. So if you have access to the project, you can see prod and staging within that project, unless you split them into separate projects.

[04:55] Ethan Morales: That’s consistent with how you do other stuff in Redwood, like usage dashboards today.

[04:59] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[05:01] Sara Nguyen: Is there a read-only role? I want finance to view, but not export. Export is the scary part.

[05:07] Naomi Feldman: There is a viewer role. Export permission is gated; not every role can export. We can share the exact permission matrix, but the intent is least privilege.

[05:20] Marcus Lin: In some orgs we see a “Billing Viewer” type role that can view aggregate spend but can’t generate exports. If you need something custom we can talk, but out of the box: view vs manage vs export are separate permissions.

[05:34] Jonah Kim: Can an org admin turn off exports entirely?

[05:38] Marcus Lin: There’s an org-level setting we’re adding for “allow exports” for certain report types. Today, in early access, it’s feature-flagged. For GA we expect a toggle plus auditing.

[05:52] Priya Desai: That’s important. We have a policy where exports have to go through a formal process.

[06:00] Naomi Feldman: Understood. For many regulated customers, they keep export permission limited to a small group and rely on audit logs for traceability.

[06:11] Ethan Morales: Where does the exported file live? Is it stored on your side, S3 or whatever?

[06:17] Kevin Osei: It’s stored in our export artifact storage, tied to your org/project, encrypted at rest. The link you get in the console is time-limited.

[06:28] Priya Desai: “Encrypted at rest” meaning server-side encryption with your keys or Redwood keys?

[06:34] Marcus Lin: For Hosted and Dedicated it’s Redwood-managed keys by default. For certain Dedicated setups we can integrate with KMS for customer-managed keys. For Private in your VPC, storage stays in your environment.

[06:52] Jonah Kim: How long is it retained?

[06:55] Kevin Osei: Default is short. I don’t want to misquote—right now it’s on the order of days, not months. The goal is: generate, download, and then it expires. The audit logs remain.

[07:12] Sara Nguyen: So I can’t generate a report and share a link two weeks later.

[07:16] Kevin Osei: Correct, not with the same link. You’d re-run the export.

[07:22] Sara Nguyen: That’s okay.

[07:24] Jonah Kim: We need to know the audit log retention. How long do you keep audit events?

[07:30] Naomi Feldman: Audit logs are part of our compliance logging. Base retention is aligned with our platform policy; for enterprise we can discuss extended retention. We can send you the retention statement that’s in our SOC 2 package.

[07:45] Priya Desai: Is there an API to retrieve audit logs? We don’t want to screenshot the console.

[07:50] Marcus Lin: Yes, audit events can be accessed via API. Many customers ship them to a SIEM. There’s also console view with filtering.

[08:02] Ethan Morales: Is the export itself accessible via API? Like can we programmatically generate it.

[08:07] Logan Wright: Yes, there’s an export job endpoint. It’s async. You create job with filters, poll status, then download when it’s ready.

[08:18] Priya Desai: If you allow API export, that’s another surface. How do you control rate limits and size?

[08:25] Logan Wright: We have bounded reports: max rows, max time range. If you ask for too much, you get a validation error telling you to narrow the window or paginate.

[08:37] Kevin Osei: Also, export generation runs in a controlled worker pool, with timeouts. We log failures as well.

[08:46] Jonah Kim: Do you audit failed exports too? That can be important.

[08:49] Kevin Osei: Yes, job_failed includes error class and reason, but we avoid logging sensitive data.

[08:57] Priya Desai: Okay. Let’s talk about RBAC boundaries more. When you say org/project, how do you prevent cross-project leakage if someone guesses an ID?

[09:07] Marcus Lin: The backend enforces authz checks server-side. IDs are not enough. We validate your session/token and check membership. We also do automated tests for cross-tenant access.

[09:20] Ethan Morales: What about “routes” across microservices? Like could route names reveal internal service names?

[09:26] Logan Wright: Route is developer-supplied or gateway-derived. If you don’t provide it, you may see “Unknown route” or a derived path from the gateway. We encourage you to set route explicitly in SDK so you control naming.

[09:41] Priya Desai: Is “Unknown route” common?

[09:44] Logan Wright: Early on, yes. If teams don’t tag it, Unknown can dominate. That’s more of an adoption thing.

[09:52] Sara Nguyen: That will mess up chargeback for us.

[09:55] Naomi Feldman: We can help you with a rollout plan. But today’s call is security, so we’ll keep it focused.

[10:03] Jonah Kim: Compliance evidence. We will ask for SOC 2 Type II, and we need evidence that audit logs exist and are immutable.

[10:12] Marcus Lin: We can provide SOC 2 report under NDA. Audit logs are write-once from the application perspective; customers can’t edit them. They’re stored in our logging system with access controls.

[10:28] Priya Desai: For export auditing specifically, we need fields: actor, time, resource, action, outcome, source IP, and ideally user agent.

[10:37] Kevin Osei: We have actor, time, resource (org/project + export job ID), action, outcome. IP and user agent are included for console sessions; for API tokens we capture the client IP as seen by our edge.

[10:56] Priya Desai: Great. Can you share an example event JSON?

[11:00] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We’ll send a sanitized example.

[11:05] Ethan Morales: Another question: does export include raw prompts or completions? Because that would be a huge risk.

[11:12] Logan Wright: No. Usage Insights export is aggregates: cost, tokens, latency percentiles, error rate, by route and model. No prompt text.

[11:26] Jonah Kim: Does it include request IDs?

[11:28] Logan Wright: Not in the export. It’s not per-request logs. It’s rollups.

[11:35] Priya Desai: Okay. Data residency. If we’re Dedicated in EU region, do exports stay in-region?

[11:43] Marcus Lin: For Dedicated, compute and storage are pinned to your region, and the export artifacts follow the region. For Hosted multi-region, it depends on where the project is provisioned. For Private, it’s yours.

[12:02] Ethan Morales: So if we pick Frankfurt for Dedicated, export objects are in Frankfurt.

[12:06] Marcus Lin: That’s the intent. We’ll confirm specifics in writing.

[12:12] Sara Nguyen: We might need US too. Then we’d have separate projects.

[12:17] Naomi Feldman: That’s typically how customers handle it.

[12:20] Jonah Kim: Can you talk about invoice reconciliation? Not security, but we’ll get asked.

[12:26] Logan Wright: The console insights are near-real-time-ish, with some late-arriving metering. It can differ slightly from invoice totals depending on cutoff and credits. For exports, we include timestamps and a note that it’s “usage insights view”, not an invoice.

[12:44] Sara Nguyen: As long as it’s consistent week over week.

[12:48] Logan Wright: That’s the goal.

[12:51] Priya Desai: Back to exports: do you support SSO and SCIM? Because export permissions are tied to roles.

[12:58] Naomi Feldman: Yes, SAML SSO for enterprise. SCIM for user provisioning. Role mapping can be set at the org level.

[13:10] Marcus Lin: And we support MFA enforcement policies too.

[13:14] Priya Desai: Nice.

[13:16] Ethan Morales: Kevin, you said export download emits audit event. What if someone shares the file after downloading. That’s out of your control.

[13:24] Kevin Osei: Correct. We only control the platform side. That’s why we focus on logging who initiated the export and the download.

[13:33] Jonah Kim: Do you have “view only” without export? Some tools have that but still allow screenshot.

[13:39] Naomi Feldman: Yeah, you can’t prevent screenshots. The control is: restrict export and keep audit logs.

[13:45] Priya Desai: Makes sense.

[13:47] Logan Wright: Also exports have size limits to prevent bulk extraction.

[13:52] Priya Desai: What are the size limits?

[13:54] Logan Wright: For GA we’re targeting max rows and max time window. Typical: up to top N routes, hourly or daily rollups. If you need more, we’d push you to the API with pagination, but still bounded.

[14:10] Sara Nguyen: We probably just need top 200 routes weekly.

[14:13] Logan Wright: That’s within the design.

[14:16] Ethan Morales: Another RBAC edge case: if a request uses smart routing and falls back to another model, is it still attributed to the same route? That affects chargeback.

[14:26] Logan Wright: Yes, route is attached at request context. Even if model changes mid-flight, we keep cost attributed to the original route. The export will show model breakdown under that route.

[14:40] Ethan Morales: Great.

[14:42] Jonah Kim: Does audit log include that it was “model breakdown export” vs “route list export”?

[14:48] Kevin Osei: It includes report type and schema version. Like “usage_insights_route_list_v1” or “route_detail_model_breakdown_v1”.

[15:01] Priya Desai: Schema versioning is good, but how do you avoid breaking our parsing.

[15:06] Logan Wright: We treat the export schema as an API contract. If we add fields, we do additive changes. If we need to change meaning, we bump version.

[15:18] Priya Desai: Okay.

[15:20] Naomi Feldman: Do you have any “must have” items for this to pass security, besides the audit schema?

[15:26] Priya Desai: The must haves: export create + download events, with IP, actor, and scope; ability to retrieve audit logs; and confirmation that exports do not contain prompts. Also data residency statement.

[15:43] Jonah Kim: And retention: audit logs at least one year for us, but we can store them ourselves if we can pull them.

[15:52] Marcus Lin: If you export audit logs to your SIEM, you can keep them as long as you want. We’ll confirm our native retention, but SIEM export is common.

[16:04] Ethan Morales: How do we export audit logs? Is that another export job? (laugh)

[16:09] Marcus Lin: No, separate endpoint. And you can stream them.

[16:15] Sara Nguyen: I want to ask: is there a way to schedule usage exports? Weekly.

[16:20] Naomi Feldman: Not built-in scheduling yet. Many customers do it via API and cron. But the security side stays the same: audit logs show the service account.

[16:32] Priya Desai: Service accounts are fine. We’d lock them down.

[16:36] Logan Wright: Exactly.

[16:38] Jonah Kim: One more: do you log failed authorization attempts? Like if someone tries to export without permission.

[16:45] Marcus Lin: We log auth failures at the API gateway level and can surface them. For audit logs, we focus on successful actions, but security logs include denied attempts.

[16:58] Priya Desai: That’s okay as long as it’s available.

[17:02] Naomi Feldman: We’ll include that nuance in the follow-up.

[17:06] Ethan Morales: Could you share the exact list of fields in audit events? This is where vendors usually hand-wave.

[17:12] Kevin Osei: Yep. I’ll send a field list. Off the top: event_name, event_time, actor_user_id, actor_email, actor_type, org_id, project_id, export_job_id, report_type, filters_json (or filter string), requested_time_range_start/end, aggregation_window, format (csv/json), outcome, row_count, bytes, client_ip, user_agent.

[17:39] Priya Desai: Perfect.

[17:41] Jonah Kim: filters_json—does that contain any PII?

[17:45] Kevin Osei: It shouldn’t, unless your route names contain it. Which we recommend against.

[17:51] Priya Desai: Understood.

[17:53] Naomi Feldman: We can also provide route naming guidance as part of implementation.

[17:58] Sara Nguyen: Ethan, we should align with our dev teams.

[18:01] Ethan Morales: Yep.

[18:03] Naomi Feldman: Okay, we’re at around 18 minutes. I’ll pause—any other compliance questions?

[18:10] Jonah Kim: SOC 2 and ISO coverage, and whether this feature is included in your controls.

[18:16] Naomi Feldman: Export auditing is part of our “logging and monitoring” controls. We’ll provide SOC 2 Type II report and a statement mapping audit logs. ISO 27001 is in progress—Marcus can confirm current status.

[18:30] Marcus Lin: We’re aligned with ISO controls; formal cert is not complete yet. SOC 2 Type II is available.

[18:40] Priya Desai: Okay.

[18:42] Ethan Morales: Last technical thing: is the export data coming from the same pipeline as billing metering? Because we worry about discrepancies.

[18:50] Logan Wright: It’s sourced from metering plus telemetry, but it’s aggregated differently and may lag. It’s for operational insights and cost drivers, not invoice. We’ll document that.

[19:05] Sara Nguyen: As long as we can explain it.

[19:08] Naomi Feldman: We have an FAQ: “why doesn’t it match invoice exactly” with reasons like late-arriving data, credits, rounding.

[19:18] Priya Desai: Great.

[19:20] Naomi Feldman: Okay, let’s jump to recap and next steps so we don’t run over.

[19:25] Naomi Feldman: Action items on Redwood: Kevin will send sample audit events and field list; Marcus will confirm retention and data residency statement for Dedicated; I’ll send the SOC 2 packet and how to retrieve audit logs; Logan will send RBAC boundary summary for insights + exports. Priya, you’ll send your internal export control requirements. Does that sound right?

[19:50] Priya Desai: Yes.

[19:51] Jonah Kim: Yes.

[19:52] Ethan Morales: Works.

[19:53] Sara Nguyen: Yep.

[19:55] Naomi Feldman: Great. Thanks everyone.
